edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Quoniam comperi nonnullos, qui se plurimum sapere suis persuasionibus credunt, insanire, bacchari, et velut quiddam promptum ex oraculo dicere: postquam esse in mundo christiana gens coepit, terrarum orbem periisse, multiformibus malis affectum esse genus humanum; ipsos etiam coelites, derelictis curis solemnibus, quibus quondam solebant invisere res nostras, terrarum ab regionibus exterminatos: statui pro captu, ac mediocritate sermonis contraire invidiae, et calumniosas dissolvere criminationes, ne aut illi sibi videantur, popularia dum verba depromunt, magnum aliquid dicere; aut, si nos talibus continuerimus a litibus, obtinuisse se causam putent, victam sui vitio, non assertorum silentio destitutam. Neque enim negaverim validissimam esse accusationem istam, hostilibusque condignos odiis nos esse, si apud nos esse constiterit causas, per quas suis mundus aberravit ab legibus, exterminati sunt dii longe, examina tanta moerorum mortalium importata sunt saeculis. Inspiciamus igitur opinionis istius mentem, et hoc quod dicitur, quale sit: summotisque omnibus contentionum studiis, quibus obscurari et contegi contemplatio rerum solet, an sit istud quod dicitur verum, momentorum parium examinatione pendamus. Efficietur enim profecto rationum consequentium copulatu, ut non impii nos magis, sed illi ipsi reperiantur criminis istius rei, qui se numinum profitentur esse cultores, atque inveteratis religionibus deditos. Ac primum ab his illud familiari et placida oratione perquirimus: postquam esse nomen in terris christianae religionis occoepit, quidnam invisitatum, quid incognitum, quid contra leges principaliter institutas, aut sensit aut passa est rerum ipsa quae dicitur appellaturque natura? Numquid in contrarias qualitates prima illa elementa mutata sunt, ex quibus res omnes consensum est esse concretas? Numquid machinae hujus, et molis, qua universi tegimur, et continemur inclusi, parte est in aliqua relaxata, aut dissoluta constructio? Numquid vertigo haec mundi, primigenii motus moderaren excedens, aut tardius repere, aut praecipiti coepit volubilitate raptari? Numquid ab occiduis partibus attolere se astra, atque in ortus fieri signorum coepta est inclinatio? Numquid ipse siderum sol princeps, cujus omnia luce vestiuntur, atque animantur calore, exarsit, intepuit, atque in contrarios habitus moderaminis soliti temperamenta corrupit? Numquid luna desivit redintegrare se ipsam, atque in veteres formas novellarum semper restitutione traducere? Numquid frigora, numquid calores, numquid tepores medii inaequalium temporum confusionibus occiderunt? Numquid longos habere dies bruma, revocare tardissimas luces nox coepit aestatis? Numquid suas animas expiraverunt venti? emortiusque flaminibus neque coelum coactatur in nubila, nec madidata ex imbribus arva succedunt? Commendata semina tellus recusat accidere, aut frondescere arbores nolunt? sapor frugibus esculentis, et vitis liquoribus mutatus est? olearum ex bacculis cruor teter exprimitur, nec lumini subministratur extincto? Animalia terris sueta, atque in aquis degentia non suriunt, nec concipiunt? foetus non in uteris sumptos suis moribus, et sua lege custodiunt? Ipsi homines denique, quos per inhabitabiles oras terrae sparsit prima incipiensque navitas, non matrimonia copulant nuptiarum solennibus justis? non dulcissimas procreant liberorum stirpes, non negotia publica, non privata, et familiares res agunt?
pass_a_gloss: Since I have discovered that some people, who believe themselves to be very wise in their own persuasions, are raving, being frenzied, and as if something ready from an oracle is being said: after the Christian people began to exist in the world, the earth has perished, the human race has been affected by many evils; even the heavenly beings, having abandoned their solemn cares, by which they were accustomed to visit our affairs, have been exterminated from the regions of the earth: I have decided, according to my ability and the mediocrity of my speech, to oppose the envy and to dissolve the calumnious accusations, so that neither they may seem to themselves to be saying something great while they utter popular words, nor, if we were to restrain ourselves from such disputes, they may think that they have obtained their case, which has been conquered by their own fault, not by the silence of those who assert it. For I will not deny that this accusation is very strong, and that we are worthy of hostile hatreds, if it is established that there are causes among us, by which the world has strayed from its laws, the gods have been exterminated, and so many mortal misfortunes have been imported into the ages. Let us therefore examine the mind of this opinion, and what is being said, and, having set aside all the contentious studies, by which the contemplation of things is accustomed to be obscured and covered, let us weigh whether what is being said is true by an examination of equal moments. For it will certainly be brought about by the conjunction of consequent reasons, that not we, but they themselves, who profess to be cultivators of the divine and dedicated to ancient religions, will be found to be guilty of this crime. And first, we ask this from them in a familiar and peaceful speech: after the name of the Christian religion began to exist on earth, what unseen, what unknown, what contrary to the laws principally instituted has the nature of things itself, which is called and is said to be, either perceived or suffered? Have the first elements, from which all things are agreed to be composed, been changed into contrary qualities? Has any part of the machine and structure of the universe, by which we are covered and contained, been relaxed or dissolved? Has the rotation of the world, which moderates the primordial motion, begun to proceed more slowly or more quickly, or has it started to be seized by a precipitous volatility? Has the inclination of the stars, which rise from the western parts and are made into signs in the east, begun to occur? Has the sun, the prince of the stars, whose light clothes and animates all things, become inflamed, grown cold, and corrupted the temperaments of its usual moderation? Has the moon ceased to renew itself and to be led back into its old forms by the restitution of new moons? Have the cold, the heat, and the moderate temperatures of unequal times perished in confusion? Has the winter begun to have long days and to recall the latest lights of the night in summer? Have the winds expired their souls? And has the flame, being dead, not forced the sky into clouds, nor have the fields, moistened by rains, succeeded? Does the earth refuse to receive the seeds that have been entrusted to it, or do the trees not want to sprout? Has the taste of edible fruits and the liquid of wines been changed? Does the blood of olives, expressed from their berries, not provide light when it is extinguished? Do the animals, which are accustomed to the earth and dwell in the waters, not suckle, nor do they conceive? Do the fetuses, which have been taken up in the wombs, not keep their customs and their law? Do men, finally, whom the first and beginning navigation has scattered over the uninhabitable shores of the earth, not join in marriages with the solemnities of just nuptials? Do they not produce the sweetest offspring of children, nor do they conduct public, private, and domestic affairs?

pass_b_english: I have found that certain people, convinced of their own superior wisdom, are actually raving and frenzied, spouting pronouncements as if they came straight from an oracle. They claim that ever since the Christian people appeared in the world, the earth has perished and the human race has been afflicted by every kind of evil. They even assert that the heavenly beings have abandoned their solemn duty of watching over our affairs and have been driven from the regions of the earth. Accordingly, I have decided — within the limits of my ability and my modest rhetorical skill — to counter this malicious envy and refute these slanderous accusations. I do this so that these accusers cannot delude themselves into thinking they are saying something profound merely by uttering popular slogans, nor can they claim victory by default if we remain silent, as if our silence proved their case rather than their own fault.

I will not deny that their accusation carries great weight, nor that we would deserve hostile hatred — if it were established that we are the cause of the world straying from its laws, of the gods being exterminated, and of such vast misfortunes being imported into human history. Let us therefore examine the mindset behind this opinion and test the truth of what is said. Setting aside all contentious wrangling that only obscures reality, let us weigh the claim on a balance of equal evidence. The logical consequence will inevitably show that the guilty parties are not us, but those very people who profess to be worshipers of the divine and devotees of ancient religion.

First, I put this question to them in a calm and reasonable tone: since the name of the Christian religion began to exist on earth, what has nature itself — the world we see and experience — either perceived or suffered that is unseen, unknown, or contrary to the fundamental laws established at the beginning? Have the primary elements, from which all things are composed, been altered into opposite qualities? Has any part of the cosmic machine that encloses and sustains us been loosened or dissolved? Has the rotation of the world, which governs the primordial motion, begun to run slower or faster, or has it been seized by a wild, precipitous volatility? Have the stars begun to rise in the west and set in the east, reversing their appointed courses? Has the sun, the prince of the stars, whose light clothes all things and whose heat animates them, flared up or grown cold, corrupting the temperate balance of its usual governance? Has the moon ceased to renew itself, failing to return to its old phases through the cycle of new moons? Have cold, heat, and the moderate temperatures of the seasons perished in confusion? Has winter begun to have long days, and has night begun to recall the late dawns of summer? Have the winds breathed their last? And, with the winds dead, has the sky not been forced into clouds, and have rain-soaked fields not followed? Does the earth refuse to receive the seeds entrusted to it, or do the trees refuse to sprout? Has the flavor of edible fruits and the juice of the vine been changed? Does the oil pressed from olives no longer feed the lamp when it is extinguished? Do land animals and sea creatures no longer suckle or conceive? Do fetuses in the womb no longer develop according to their natural law? Finally, do human beings — scattered by the earliest navigation to the remotest shores — no longer join in marriage with the solemn rites of just nuptials? Do they no longer produce the sweetest offspring of children, nor conduct public, private, and domestic affairs?

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the rhetorical questions and the complex conditional structures of the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent, high-quality English version that preserves all nuances of the original, including the specific scientific/natural observations (astronomy, botany, biology) used by Arnobius.
